title: Gazans face near-daily Israeli strikes a year into ceasefire
content: More than 1,400 people in Gaza have been killed in Israeli attacks since the start of the ceasefire on 10 October last year, according to Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. The ceasefire saw thousands of Palestinians held by Israel released in return for the remaining hostages held in Gaza. It was an agreement to end the war, triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage. But even during the ceasefire, Israel has continued launching strikes in Gaza almost every day. Israel says it is targeting Hamas operatives and accuses Hamas of continued violations of the ceasefire. The total death toll from Israeli attacks since the start of the war in Gaza now stands at more than 74,000, according to the Gaza health ministry. Israel blocks international journalists from going in to Gaza to report freely. With the help of journalists in Gaza, Yogita Limaye reports from Jerusalem. Read more here. An aeroplane flying to Israel fell 17,000ft (5,200m) in less than two minutes before it was diverted. The man says he "pulled the controls" of the plane after it plummeted during the attack. BBC Verify explains how we found the wreckage location of a Saudi F-15 fighter jet which the Iran-backed Houthi group says it shot down over Yemen. BBC's Middle East correspondent Lucy Williamson reports from an area close to Israel's proposed site in the occupied West Bank. Six people, including three pupils at the Palestinian school, have been killed in al-Mughayyir this year, in a surge of Israeli settler-related violence. Omar al-Bayoumi has always denied being an extremist and a Saudi spy. The BBC's Lucy Williamson reports on settler attacks on Palestinians, which have been observed over the last week alone. Washington announced what it described as an "economic D-Day" against Iran, widening current sanctions and targetting countries with business ties with the regime. After the homeowners made their initial report to the Israeli army, the first soldiers who arrived at the scene were filmed praying with the settlers. Republican Senator Lindsay Graham's funeral is bringing the two world leaders to town, where they'll separately visit the White House to discuss their region's wars. Israeli settlers set fire to two mosques, as well as cars and agricultural land in the occupied West Bank, Palestinian officials say. Mojtaba Khamenei hasn’t been seen in public since March - but AI-generated images of him continue to spread online. The BBC's chief international correspondent looks at how Iran's new leadership will respond to several issues affecting the country. The US has launched the strikes on Iran in response to attacks on three oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz. Huge crowds have lined the streets of Tehran for the funeral procession of Iran's late supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. The BBC's chief international correspondent Lyse Doucet is in Tehran, where funeral events are taking place in honour of Iran's former leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. Authorities expect up to 20 million people to attend ceremonies across Iran and Iraq over the coming days. Iranian authorities say they expect millions of people to take part in funeral commemorations for Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. Dozens of boats are still anchored in the Strait, while ordinary Iranians try to continue to their lives. The BBC’s Daniel Bush is traveling with Secretary of State Marco Rubio as he seeks to reassure Gulf allies over the Iran deal aimed at ending the war. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved. title: Three sisters who drowned in sea off Brighton took own lives, inquest finds
content: Three sisters who drowned in the sea off Brighton took their own lives, a coroner has ruled. Jane Adetoro, 36, Christina Walters, 32, and Rebecca Walters, 31, had been living "very secluded lives" following the death of their mother, who drowned in 2010, senior coroner Penelope Schofield said. On 11 May, the women - who had all been living together in Greenford, London - visited an area of Birmingham close to where their mother died before travelling the next day to Brighton beach, where they drowned in adverse sea conditions in the early hours of 13 May. The coroner said they could not swim. Their father Joseph Jacobsen said it was heartbreaking to lose "all three of my precious daughters". He was among family members who followed proceedings via video link. In an emotional statement read out on his behalf, he said he watched his daughters grow from little girls to beautiful, intelligent women "with a special place in my heart". He said: "There are no words that can adequately express the pain of losing a child. "To lose all three of my precious daughters is a heartbreak beyond anything I could ever have imagined." He could not understand why his daughters' lives ended so suddenly, and hoped they were reunited with their mother "in God's eternal care", he added. The coroner told the court: "These three sisters lived very secluded lives, they were incredibly private, we don't know why they took this course of action or indeed why they chose to do it in Brighton. "It is not for the court to speculate and sadly these reasons may never be known." The hearing was told the sisters left their home in London and arrived in Brighton together by taxi at 22:21 BST on 12 May. The Uber driver had noted the lack of conversation during their journey. The three appeared to pace the seafront in the darkness, with CCTV sightings of them at different points along Brighton's east beach. They were last seen alive at 02:42 on 13 May. Police searched Christina's laptop and found 227 references to water and 179 references to suicide. The coroner said Christina had been experiencing anxiety and depression since the death of her mother. Rebecca's medical records showed "nothing of note" and Jane was not registered with a doctor, Det Ch Insp Mark Cullimore told the court. A previous inquest into their mother's death had found her cause of death was drowning. Postmortem tests revealed toxicology results for all three sisters were negative for drugs and alcohol. There was no evidence to suggest they had been subject to violence. Ms Adetoro was brought to shore by an RNLI crew and declared dead at the scene on the morning of 13 May, the inquest heard. Christina Walters, who worked in accountancy, was recovered from the sea by an RNLI lifeboat, and Rebecca Walters, who worked in HR, was washed on to the shore of Brighton beach. They were also pronounced dead that morning by paramedics. Follow BBC Sussex on Facebook , X , and Instagram and listen to BBC Radio Sussex on Sounds . title: Suspect linked to Monaco bomb attack on millionaire speaks to BBC from Ukrainian prison
content: A former Ukrainian security services officer linked to a bomb attack in Monaco in June that targeted a multi-millionaire says he believed it was ordered by senior members of HUR, Ukraine's military intelligence agency. In an exclusive interview with the BBC from prison in Kyiv, facilitated by his lawyer, Vitalii Zhykovych has given his own account of the attempted assassination for the first time. Ukrainian-born businessman Vadym Yermolayev and his 13-year-old son were badly hurt in the blast and his partner suffered catastrophic injuries. Yermolayev later described their survival as "nothing short of a miracle". Zhykovych describes himself as a "freelancer" for Ukraine's SBU security service and says Anastasia Berezovska, the woman caught on camera planting the bomb in Monaco, was his "agent". A week after the bombing, Berezovska's body was discovered in the woods west of Kyiv with gunshot wounds to the head. But Zhykovych insists he did not send her to kill, and nor did he kill her. He was arrested and accused of her murder together with an active-duty intelligence officer from HUR called Vladyslav Reut. Reut initially confessed to investigators, and led them to the shallow grave. But days later in court, he changed his testimony to blame Zhykovych. For a long time, Zhykovych himself stayed silent. Now, responding to questions from the BBC, he alleges that Reut - who he refers to as "The Boss" - had "proposed the operation" in Monaco against Vadym Yermolayev. He understood it was an official mission. "As Reut informed me, this operation […] had been authorised and approved by Reut's superiors, who served in the Main Intelligence Directorate of the Ministry of Defence [HUR]," he says. Distancing himself from the explosion itself, he alleges that Reut asked to use Berezovska for the bombing and when Zhykovych refused – he says she was not fully trained – Reut agreed to send her for reconnaissance instead. Reut then communicated directly with Bereszovska without including him, according to Zhykovych, who alleges that Reut also provided her with the explosives. The BBC asked HUR to comment on the latest claims. The agency has previously said that it is "committed to a full investigation" and providing "comprehensive support" to law enforcement bodies. The SBU has described Zhykovych in a statement only as a "former law enforcement officer". Yermolayev was attacked in Monaco as he and his family were returning from an evening meal on the seafront. A surveillance video shows Berezovska walking slightly in front of the group, then leaving the device in a bag on their doorstep. It detonates just as they get close, apparently shocking even Berezovska with its force. Yermolayev later said he believed that serving HUR officers, "individuals close to the agency's current and former leadership", were linked to the attack. He called for "the truth, protection, and justice". Berezovska was quickly identified as the suspected bomber and on 2 July her image, taken from CCTV footage, was circulated by Interpol. She had already fled, first driving through Italy and Germany, then taking a bus from Frankfurt to Ukraine. Before she could be caught and questioned though, she was driven to the woods by Reut and Zhykovych and killed. Each blames the other for her shooting. The shocking case has prompted intense speculation, including over who may have wanted Yermolayev dead and why, and whether this could have been a state-ordered assassination attempt, a rogue operation or some kind of criminal score-settling. The businessman himself, who renounced his Ukrainian passport some years ago and now has Cypriot citizenship, has dismissed multiple theories. They include the idea the attack might be linked to a struggle between organised crime groups involved in highly lucrative scam call-centres in Ukraine. Earlier this year, a court in Estonia convicted Yermolayev's son, Artur, of defrauding its citizens out of millions of euros through such "offisy", as the scam networks are known in Ukraine. Vadym Yermolayev told the Ukrainska Pravda newspaper that he "never had anything to do with anything" in the case. Now Zhykovych has put forward his own theory to us. He alleges that Reut told him the bombing was in retaliation for "funding the annexation of Crimea", which he understood to mean Yermolayev was paying taxes to Russia from businesses in Russian-occupied Crimea. "In my view, this constitutes grounds for the operation," he communicated from prison. Yermolayev has repeatedly denied any remaining business interests linked to Russia. But might this story be even murkier? At his most recent custody hearing in Kyiv, surrounded by heavily armed guards, Zhykovych spoke publicly for the first time since his arrest. The BBC were the only media present. At one point Zhykovych said Reut had in fact told him the attack in Monaco was not "authorised". "Someone had ordered this target from the civilian side," Zhykovych said, without explaining. The judge then interrupted, reminding him that he was addressing an open court. Zhykovych also revealed that Reut originally talked of two targets. When we asked, he said he could not disclose the second name. Other sources strongly suggest it was a pro-Russian blogger tried and convicted in absentia last year by Ukraine of treason. As the investigation continues – into both the bombing in Monaco and the murder in Ukraine - Berezovska's family have many questions of their own. The 39-year-old had been in Germany since early 2022, when she left Ukraine as a refugee with her young son. Zhykovych now claims she was living a double-life, working with him as an agent "against Muscovy" – meaning Russia. He said they had met online and told us the pair were working to "repel the armed aggression of the Russian Federation". Berezovska's husband has told the BBC that the allegation was "nonsense". He believes she was dragged, unwittingly, into the whole affair. Zhykovych says Berezovska called him the day after the Monaco attack, and when he asked why she had done it, she said Reut had promised her a huge fee. "$50,000 doesn't just lie on the streets," she supposedly explained. Residents in her village have told us that Berezovska was saving to buy a flat. But when she travelled to Ukraine to collect the money, she was lured into the woods and shot. Additional reporting by Anastasiia Levchenko and Volodymyr Lozhko. It is the latest in a diplomatic spat after Kyiv disclosed that two North Korean prisoners were transferred to Seoul. Five children are among the victims of a strike that destroyed 30 flats in northern Ukraine as families slept. Ukrainians travelling by train are increasingly caught in the crosshairs of Russia's attacks. Arkadii Petrov - who attended Kirkcudbright Academy - is honoured at the Ukrainian Chapel in Lockerbie. The vessel's captain was killed and 11 crew members were rescued after the attack on the Turkish-owned ship, Ukraine's leader says. Copyright 2026 BBC. All rights reserved.
